timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Mr. Vice President, welcome to New Hampshire Round Table.
Glad to join you.
It's great to have you.
You're obviously in a tight race here in New Hampshire.
The polls indicate you're just underbilled Bradley.
What are you going to do about that?
Well, I think that's healthy for New Hampshire and for the country.
And don't get me wrong, I've run unopposed and opposed,
and I prefer unopposed.
But I know that even though I might prefer that,
this really is a good thing because it has already made it
easier for me to see the need to make changes in my campaign operation.
I move the headquarters to Tennessee and we've cut it by 50%.
I'm getting rid of some of the accoutrements of the office of Vice President
that I was hampered with before.
And I'm just having open meetings and talking to people in small groups
straight from the heart.
And I've been enjoying it, really.
I believe you've called yourself an underdog here in New Hampshire.
That must have been quite a surprise to you.
You were such a strong leader from the outset with the institution behind you
of the White House.
What have you learned from this?
Well, I thought that if he crossed the threshold of credibility, which he did,
I thought that it would be inevitable that a two person race would tighten and narrow.
It's like Coca-Cola and Pepsi-Cola.
And so it's not a total surprise.
And I also learned how to be more effective as a candidate
and how to connect with the audiences that I address and the people that I talk with.
And in the campaigns I've run in the past, I've gone through a similar learning experience,
but it's often been the final four or five weeks of the campaign before I really feel
like I'm campaigning as effectively as I can.
And due to the competition and due to the closeness of the race,
I've been able to get there a year early and I'm grateful for that.
Many people who know you say you're not the stiff wooden character
that the press often portrays you as.
Why don't you show more of the softer, funnier side to the public?
Well, I am who I am and I can't change that.
I don't want to change that.
And I guess it's in the eye of the beholder.
I think I learned from my father years ago a little bit of a more formal manner in public,
but I think as I get older it's easier for me to be in large groups the same way I am
with my close friends.
And that's a better and easier way to campaign also.
One of the things that really interests me about you is your relationship with your father,
the former Tennessee Senator Albert Gore.
I believe your father wanted you to be president, had ambitions for you.
Some say that you're running more for him than for yourself.
Is there a grain of truth in that?
No, none whatsoever.
And in fact neither of my parents who've been described as ambitions on my behalf,
neither of them ever tried to encourage me to go into politics.
In fact, both of them were surprised when I did.
Because my life was, but she helped me win that race.
And it was the beginning of the last 23 years of public service.
Now that you're working on this more accessible image, may I call you out?
You can, you know Paul Simon wrote a song with exactly that title.
So, feel free.
Thank you very much.
I really appreciate your time.
Glad to do it.

youtube_description:
Now that we're faced with Al Gore's Inconvenient Sequel, it's tempting to ask: What if he had actually won the Presidential election back in 2000? 
Remember when the century turned, the chads clung and hung, Florida was in Republican hands, and the Supreme Court ended up deciding the race in favor of the fortunate son of George H.W. Bush? Well, how many wayward chads would it have taken to give us 4 years of Al Gore? For one thing, I don't think we'd have pulled out of the Paris Climate Accord. But what else might have -- or have not happened?
I had the chance to interview the Vice President for NHPTV in the autumn of 1999, prior to the New Hampshire Presidential Primary. Little did I know of what was to come, or I might have asked  different questions...
